messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Nadia Haddad was 36 when she was hospitalized with a rapidly worsening illness that left her convinced, more than once, that she might die. She had been working long shifts on a construction site, used to trusting her body and priding herself on being able to keep up with men who underestimated her, when she developed symptoms that escalated frighteningly fast. In the emergency department she remembers monitors sounding, staff moving quickly around her, and the unmistakable look on her husband’s face when he was told to wait outside while they stabilized her. What has stayed with her most is the sense that her body had become dangerous and unpredictable without warning. She had gone in as someone strong and capable; she came out feeling that catastrophe could break through at any moment and that there was nothing she could do to stop it.

In the weeks after discharge, Nadia did return to work, but she no longer experienced her body as reliable. On site, the clang of dropped metal or the sudden revving of machinery made her jolt hard enough that coworkers noticed. At night she struggled to fall asleep and woke repeatedly, already tense, as if braced for an alarm no one else could hear. Much of the day her muscles stayed tight and ready, and she watched herself react to ordinary sensations with a kind of dread. These reactions frightened her in their own right. Lying awake with her heart racing, or catching herself jumping at a noise, she had come to believe that something in her mind was giving way. If she could not calm down, if her body stayed this wound up all the time, maybe she was going crazy. The persistence of it also fed a darker conviction: if danger could erupt inside her once and leave her this changed, then she had no real future to count on and no way to stop bad things from happening to her.

Those beliefs began to shape how she managed her days. When she felt trapped by the thought that she was losing her mind, or by the certainty that nothing good lay ahead, Nadia did not try to sit with the fear. She stayed late at work, volunteered for extra tasks, and threw herself into physically demanding jobs to keep her mind occupied. The construction site became more than employment; it was a place where there was always something to carry, measure, or fix, and as long as she was moving she did not have to think as much. At home, when the dread pushed through anyway, she ate past hunger because the heaviness and routine of eating blunted her enough to get through the evening. She also described going emotionally flat with her husband, not because she felt nothing mattered, but because numbing herself seemed safer than letting the panic and despair fully in.

Her sense of constant alarm also drove these habits. After a day of jumping at noises and feeling her body stay keyed up, overworking felt like the only way to outrun the agitation, and overeating became a quick way to dull the edge of it at night. Yet the relief never lasted. The more she lived this way, the more she read it as evidence that something was fundamentally wrong with her. Seeing herself unable to rest, unable to stop filling every hour, unable to face her feelings without eating or shutting down, Nadia became even more certain that she was going crazy. When she went emotionally numb with her husband and could not explain what was happening inside her, she took that distance as further proof that the illness had ruined her life and left her without a future she could trust.

Over the following months, the pattern tightened. Poor sleep left her more jumpy the next day; the jumpiness confirmed her fear that she was no longer in control; and that fear pushed her harder into work and further into numbing routines that kept her from feeling anything directly. Her husband began urging her to slow down, but she heard this less as concern than as confirmation that he could see her changing. She ate in secret sometimes, ashamed of how desperate she felt for distraction, then lay awake tense and discouraged, telling herself that if she were stronger she would be able to stop this. A small part of her still noticed how relentless it all had become.

Nadia finally sought help after startling violently at work when a steel beam was dropped nearby and having to hide in a portable office until she could steady herself. What shook her most was not only the reaction itself, but the thought that followed immediately: this is never going to end, and I am becoming someone I do not recognize. She came to treatment frightened that she is losing her mind and that another disaster could strike at any time, but also hoping, cautiously, that if someone could help her understand why she has been living in a state of constant alarm, she might still have a future that feels like her own.
